reason: NTC is under DICT, not DOST; DOST isn't telecom regulator.
en: DOST and NTC notices sometimes describe emergency communication support when typhoons cut ordinary phone networks, a technical help communities need.

reason: PAGASA bulletins give weather track, not official support advice.
en: Compare this morning's PAGASA bulletin with yesterday's to see how official support advice changed as the track shifted toward or away from a province.

reason: PAGASA warns; PCG enforces sea travel suspensions, not PAGASA.
en: PCG or PAGASA marine notices that stop sea travel are support for coastal workers, a safety action you can copy from those official marine pages.

reason: Capacity factor is energy output ratio, not time useful.
en: Energy tables often list a capacity factor for tidal sites; that number, from a secondary source, tells how much of the time the difference is useful.

reason: Tidal fences use fast currents, not water-level difference.
en: Some papers describe tidal fences, rows of turbines across part of a channel, another situation for exploiting fast tidal difference without a full dam.

reason: Suitability depends on data, not source type.
en: A strait can look fast from a boat yet fail a resource map's speed and depth cuts; the secondary source, not the boat trip, decides suitability.

reason: Slack water means weak current, not small tidal range.
en: Because output follows the tide, some studies pair tidal plants with storage so electricity is still available when the difference is small at slack water.

reason: Not a science fact; citation advice too advanced for grade 5.
en: When you call a mutation beneficial or harmful, write the textbook or journal you used, because the same DNA change can be judged differently in another environment.

reason: Mutations don't relocate; 'later sits in a gene' is misleading.
en: A change that does nothing in a unused DNA stretch can be harmful if it later sits in a gene that an organism needs, so context matters.

reason: High-altitude adaptation involves oxygen-sensing genes, not hemoglobin variants.
en: Some human populations have hemoglobin variants that help at high altitude, beneficial mutations studied in secondary genetics sources.

reason: Effect depends on environment, but sources don't always name it.
en: The same mutation can be beneficial in one habitat and harmful in another, so sources always name the environment when they assign an effect.

reason: Helpful/harmful/neutral classification isn't always tied to named environment.
en: In one sentence: mutations change DNA, and sources classify those changes as helpful, harmful, or neither, always in a named environment.

reason: Says four boxes right; actually three moves from boron to oxygen.
en: From boron in group 13, count four boxes right to oxygen in group 16: 13, 14, 15, 16, matching four, five, then six valence electrons.

reason: Ozone's shared electrons give each O an octet, not six.
en: In ozone each oxygen atom still has six valence electrons; the molecule's shape changes, not the group-16 outer count of each atom.

reason: Oxygen is fourth among B through Ne, not sixth.
en: Moving left to right across period 2, each step adds one valence electron, so oxygen, sixth among B through Ne, has six.

reason: Assumes constant rate/direction for 50 Ma; needs uncertainty caveat.
en: Draw today's motion as an arrow on a map of the Philippines, then extend that arrow to represent 50 million years at the same rate.

reason: Video is a recording tool, not a model; forces aren't directly visible.
en: A slow-motion phone video is a model of the short contact time, letting you describe the push during the hit without guessing the forces.

reason: Not a science fact; report-order instruction, not content.
en: When gathering sources, list vehicle systems first: belt, bag, crumple zone, then extras, so the report matches the competency's named examples.

reason: Bumper-height rules mainly prevent override/underride; crumple-zone link oversimplified.
en: Bumper-height standards in source documents try to make collisions meet at the same level so energy goes into designed crumple structures.

reason: Not a factual claim; source task too advanced.
en: Gather at least two official or test-lab sources, then identify seatbelts, airbags, crumple zones, and one extra device, each with a short because.

reason: Equation shown is unbalanced; needs coefficients.
en: A method check is to write 'hydrogen plus oxygen yields water' then H2 + O2 → H2O, showing the same reaction in words and in formulas.

reason: Instructional jargon, not a factual science statement.
en: The competency wants both forms: if you only write formulas, add a word line; if you only write words, add the formula line scientists use.

reason: Rusting also needs water; iron oxide is simplified.
en: Write iron plus oxygen yields iron oxide in words, then the formula form, so a common rusting reaction is described the way scientists do.

reason: Sun isn't eaten; food chains start with producers.
en: A food chain shows the order in which living things eat each other, starting with the Sun and ending with a top animal.

reason: Sun isn't eaten; chains vary, not always carnivore.
en: A simple food chain always starts with the Sun, then a plant, then a herbivore, and finally a carnivore.

reason: Same object may change permanently; repeats aren't independent.
en: Repeating the same press three times on the same object shows whether the change is the same each time, making the result reliable.

reason: Movement depends on mass/friction, not just softness.
en: To compare soft and rigid objects, use the same push for both and record which one moves farther or changes shape more.

reason: Hand push force varies; use a spring scale.
en: Using the same hand push for every object keeps the force the same, so only the object's material is being tested.

reason: Growth rate slowed mainly due to fertility decline, not planetary limits.
en: The human population on Earth is still growing, but its growth rate has slowed down as we get closer to the planet's limits.

reason: Need P and S wave time difference, not just first wave arrival.
en: Scientists find an earthquake's epicenter by comparing how early the first wave arrives at three or more different seismic stations.

reason: Only maximum static friction usually exceeds moving friction; static friction varies.
en: Static friction is the force that holds the block still until the pull becomes strong enough, and it is always bigger than the friction while moving.

reason: Wave maker speed ambiguous; energy also depends on amplitude.
en: In a ripple tank, scientists keep the water depth the same and change only the wave maker's speed to see how wave energy spreads.

reason: Numbers can invert; energy or biomass decreases more reliably.
en: The number of living things usually gets smaller at each step of a food chain, so there are more plants than herbivores and more herbivores than carnivores.

reason: Algae are not true plants, though they are producers.
en: A food chain always has a producer, which is a green plant, but the plant can be a tree, grass, or algae.

reason: Not all chains end with predators; some end with herbivores.
en: A food chain always ends with a top predator that nothing else eats in that chain, like a crocodile in a river.

reason: Philippine Sea Plate lies east of, not carrying, eastern Philippines.
en: The Philippine Sea Plate is a tectonic plate under the Pacific Ocean that carries the eastern Philippines and moves northwestward toward the Asian mainland.

reason: Most islands sit on deforming Philippine Mobile Belt, not split between plates.
en: The eastern islands ride the Philippine Sea Plate while the western islands ride the Eurasian Plate, so the two sides of the archipelago move at different speeds.

reason: Plate motion changes over millions of years; 'same drift' oversimplifies.
en: Fifty million years ago, the crust that now carries the Philippine islands was in a different part of the ocean, and the same drift that moved it then moves it now.

reason: Directly east is Philippine Sea Plate, not Pacific Plate.
en: The Pacific Plate pushes from the east while the Eurasian Plate resists from the west, so the archipelago is slowly compressed between them.

reason: Returning to shape, not speed, shows elasticity.
en: Using a stopwatch, a class times how long a squeezed sponge takes to return to its full shape, which shows if it is elastic.

reason: Dent may recover after pressure removed; measure while pressed.
en: A class uses a plastic ruler to press on a soft object, then measures the depth of the dent with a ruler after removing the pressure.

reason: Only if air or open tube; completely full water won't rise.
en: A class squeezes a plastic bottle filled with water and watches the water level rise, showing how the shape change affects the inside.

reason: Air is matter touching object; wind is contact force.
en: A class uses a fan to blow air on different objects and observes which ones move, showing that force can move objects without touching them.

reason: Ignores life in ocean water and air.
en: All known life on Earth lives in or on the crust, from the deepest ocean floor to the highest mountain peak.

reason: Sedimentary top not always present; layering oversimplified.
en: Continental crust has a layered structure: a top of sedimentary rock, a middle of granite, and a deeper layer of denser rock.

reason: Noon height change varies by latitude; not 47° everywhere.
en: The Sun's noon height changes by about 47 degrees between the June and December solstices, because the tilt moves the Sun's direct rays from 23.5 degrees north to 23.5 degrees south.

reason: Closer to equator, overhead dates are farther apart, not closer.
en: The dates when the Sun is directly overhead depend on latitude, so places closer to the equator have their two overhead days closer together in the year.

reason: Crowding makes mates easier to find; growth slows from resource limits.
en: When a population gets crowded, finding a mate becomes harder, so fewer babies are born and the population's growth slows down.

reason: Water doesn't melt; it lowers rock melting temperature.
en: At a subduction zone, the sinking oceanic plate drags water and sediment into the hot mantle, where they melt and change.

reason: Philippine Sea Plate is mostly oceanic; continental pieces uncertain.
en: The Philippine Sea Plate carries both oceanic crust and small pieces of continental crust, so one plate can hold two crust types.

reason: Vehicle motors aren't directly connected by long power lines.
en: Generators are usually placed at power plants, while motors are inside homes and vehicles, so they are connected by long power lines.

reason: Volcanic rocks cool from lava at surface, not underground magma.
en: The upper crust is the source of most volcanic rocks on land, such as andesite and rhyolite, which cool from magma underground.

reason: Force should be x-axis, distance y-axis.
en: A class plots a line graph with force on the left and distance moved on the bottom to see how pushing harder makes an object go farther.

reason: Water is a raw material; cannot be controlled if testing water.
en: A fair test of photosynthesis raw materials keeps light, temperature, and water the same while changing only the one raw material being tested.

reason: Iodine test is qualitative, not a measurable amount.
en: A bar graph of the results shows the amount of starch for each condition, making the comparison easy to see.

reason: Tracing moving coils by hand is impractical; use a marker or snapshot.
en: To record a wave's shape, lay a long paper under the slinky and trace the outline of the coils as the wave passes.

reason: Limewater turns cloudy/milky, not a color change.
en: The limewater test shows a gas by a color change, while the silver nitrate test shows a solid forming from two liquids.

reason: Open load itself would read source voltage, not zero.
en: If the voltmeter reads zero across one load in a series circuit, that load is likely shorted or the circuit has a break.

reason: Tongue rolling isn't a simple single-gene dominant trait.
en: Being able to roll the tongue is a dominant trait, so a child who cannot roll the tongue must have two recessive alleles for that trait.

reason: Ambiguous: no plate boundary, but crust type changes.
en: The east coast of the United States has oceanic and continental crust sitting side by side on the same plate, with no boundary between them.

reason: Continent doesn't scrape off; it collides and crumples, resisting subduction.
en: When a continent riding on a sinking plate reaches the trench, it does not go under; it scrapes off and stays at the surface.

reason: Overriding plate is Philippine Mobile Belt, not Philippine Sea Plate.
en: Mount Pinatubo in Luzon erupted because the South China Sea floor is sinking beneath the Philippine plate at the Manila Trench.

reason: Density, not just thinness, is key for subduction.
en: Oceanic lithosphere is thinner and bends more easily, which is why it can dive into the mantle at subduction zones.

reason: Limewater is qualitative; PAGASA uses instruments, not limewater, for CO2 monitoring.
en: PAGASA scientists bubble air samples through limewater to check for carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere over time.

reason: Blowing into limewater tests limewater, not soda lime freshness.
en: The investigator checks that the soda lime is fresh by blowing through a straw into limewater to see if it still turns milky.

reason: Cutting after testing doesn't ensure fair starch patch comparison.
en: The investigator cuts the leaf into equal-sized pieces after testing to compare the starch patches fairly.

reason: Connection order isn't functionally required; any order works.
en: When assembling a circuit, connect the positive terminal of the battery to the switch first, then to the rest of the circuit.

reason: Added mass changes friction; surface/wheels alone don't equalize it.
en: A fair momentum test keeps the same floor surface and the same wheels on the cart, so friction stays equal for every trial.

reason: Friction also increases with mass; stopping distance may not rise.
en: A graph of stopping distance against mass, at the same speed, shows a rising line: more mass means a longer stop.

reason: Same mark controls height/energy, not starting speed; cart starts at rest.
en: Releasing the cart from the exact same mark on the ramp each time keeps the starting speed the same across repeated trials.

reason: Freckles are not a simple single-gene dominant trait.
en: Freckles are a dominant trait, so a child with one freckle allele from a parent will have freckles.

reason: Dimple inheritance is not a simple one-gene dominant trait.
en: Dimples are a dominant trait, so a child with one dimple allele will have dimples even if the other allele is for no dimples.

reason: Cleft chin inheritance is more complex than single-gene dominant.
en: A cleft chin is dominant over a smooth chin, so a child needs only one cleft-chin allele to have that chin shape.

reason: Hitchhiker's thumb is not a simple single-gene recessive trait.
en: A hitchhiker's thumb is a recessive trait, so a child must have two copies of the allele to have that bendy thumb.

reason: Excess CO2 can clear limewater, so cloudiness isn't linear.
en: The more carbon dioxide gas bubbled into limewater, the milkier it becomes, so cloudiness can show how much gas is present.

reason: Limewater clouds only with carbon dioxide, not all gases.
en: The time it takes for limewater to turn cloudy can be measured with a stopwatch to compare how fast different gases react.

reason: Sealing alone doesn't remove CO2; needs absorbent.
en: The setup without carbon dioxide is sealed with a rubber stopper, while the setup with carbon dioxide is left open to the room air.

reason: Angle alone doesn't set speed; release position/height also matters.
en: Setting the ramp to the same angle with a protractor keeps the starting speed the same for every trial.

reason: Sliding distance reflects energy, not momentum directly.
en: A stop block at the end of the track stops the cart, and measuring how far the block slides shows the momentum transferred.

reason: Height shows energy transfer, not momentum directly.
en: A hanging ball hit by the cart swings up, and the height it rises shows how much momentum the cart carried.

reason: Dent depth reflects energy, not momentum directly.
en: Rolling the cart into a sand-filled box makes a dent, and the depth of the dent shows how much momentum the cart had.

reason: Dent depth compares impact energy, not momentum directly.
en: Measuring the depth of the dent with a ruler gives a number that compares momentum across trials.

reason: Time alone doesn't give speed; distance is also needed.
en: Timing how long the cart takes to roll down the ramp with a stopwatch gives its speed at the bottom.

reason: Level and incline conflict; incline direction matters.
en: A level track with a slight incline slows the cart down gradually, letting you measure stopping distance easily.

reason: Momentum needs mass; app must know it.
en: A video analysis app tracks the cart's position in each frame and calculates its speed and momentum automatically.

reason: Distance depends on friction, not directly momentum.
en: A moving cart collides with a stationary cart of the same mass, and the distance the second cart moves shows the momentum transferred.

reason: Force alone doesn't show momentum; needs time or velocity.
en: Using a spring scale to pull a loaded cart up a ramp shows the force needed to overcome gravity and friction, which relates to momentum.

reason: Recipe analogy implies same ingredients both sides; only atoms balance.
en: Balancing an equation is like following a recipe: you need the same number of each ingredient on both sides, or the reaction won't match reality.

reason: Should say 'to make water,' not oxygen molecules in water.
en: The coefficients in a balanced equation give the ratio of molecules that react, like 2 hydrogen molecules for every 1 oxygen molecule in water.

reason: They grow on branches, not actually living in air.
en: Orchids that grow on tree branches high above the ground are aerial plants because they live in the air.

reason: Some snakes are aquatic, like sea snakes.
en: Snakes live on land and some climb trees, so they are terrestrial animals that do not live in water.

reason: Babies' body proportions differ from adults; oversimplified.
en: Unlike caterpillars and tadpoles, human babies look like small adults from birth, just needing to grow bigger.

reason: Wording implies butterfly hatches; actually egg hatches into caterpillar.
en: A common mistake is thinking a caterpillar is a baby butterfly, but actually the butterfly hatches from an egg as a caterpillar first.

reason: Stage counts depend on definitions; humans also have multiple stages.
en: In a flow chart, comparing life cycles side by side helps you see that butterflies and frogs have more stages than chickens and humans.

reason: Seashore is shoreline, not fully in water.
en: Habitats can be on land like a garden, or in water like a seashore, and each one has its own set of living things.

reason: Buoyancy can mask added air's weight; use rigid container.
en: To test whether air has mass, compare the balance reading of an empty sealed bag with the same bag filled with air.

reason: Cup itself has mass; subtract empty cup first.
en: Placing a cup of water on a balance shows the water has mass because the scale gives a number above zero.

reason: Insects pollinate flowers, not typically spread mango/papaya seeds.
en: Fruit trees in a garden, like mango and papaya, give food to bats, birds, and insects that help spread their seeds.

reason: Stopping distance also depends on stopping force, not momentum alone.
en: A dynamics cart with low-friction wheels rolls almost freely, so its stopping distance mainly shows its momentum rather than wheel friction.

reason: Seaweed is algae, not a true plant.
en: Seaweed grows attached to rocks underwater, so it is an aquatic plant that does not need soil.

reason: Algae/seaweed are not true plants, though plant-like.
en: Seaweed and algae are plants that grow on seashore rocks, and they provide food for small animals like sea snails.

reason: Example mixes trunks with leaves/roots; mangroves known for roots.
en: To tell plants apart in a habitat, look at their leaves and roots, because sea grasses have long blades while mangrove trees have tall trunks.

reason: Stage counts vary; human often four, not fixed five.
en: A butterfly and a frog each have four stages in their life cycle, while a chicken has three and a human has five.

reason: Chicken egg, chick, adult aren't all similar-looking.
en: Butterflies go through complete metamorphosis, meaning they have four very different-looking stages, while chickens have only three similar-looking stages.

reason: PAR is a polygon, not a rectangle.
en: The PAR boundary is drawn as a rectangle on the tracking map, so a typhoon is inside when its plotted position falls within that box.

reason: Arrows show storm movement, not wind direction.
en: Arrows on a tracking map show wind direction at each position, helping forecasters see how the typhoon is turning.

reason: Real forecasts use models, not just straight-line extrapolation.
en: To predict the next position, forecasters extend the straight line of the recent track in the same direction at the same speed.

reason: Compass isn't needed for plotting positions or track line.
en: A pencil, ruler, and compass are used to plot typhoon positions and draw the track line on a paper map.

reason: Science supports or rejects; 'prove' is too strong.
en: A hypothesis is a testable guess, so the plan must include steps that can prove it right or wrong.

reason: Fairness needs same temperature, not just simultaneous measurement.
en: Warm liquids expand, so measure temperature and volume at the same time to keep the comparison fair.

reason: Forecasters often connect points with line segments; smooth curve may misrepresent.
en: A forecaster draws a smooth curve through the plotted points, rather than connecting them with straight segments, to show the typhoon's continuous path.

reason: Estimates are approximate, not exact; interpolation gives approximate position.
en: When a typhoon's coordinates fall between grid lines, a forecaster estimates its exact position by dividing the space between the lines evenly.

reason: Rainbands are spiral, not a circle around the eye.
en: A forecaster may draw a circle around the plotted eye to show the typhoon's outer rainbands on the tracking map.

reason: Mechanical and chemical digestion often occur simultaneously, not fixed order.
en: Digestion follows a fixed order: mechanical breakdown, chemical digestion, absorption, and elimination, with each step preparing for the next.

reason: Epicenters approximate boundaries, not exact lines.
en: The pattern of earthquake epicenters across the Philippines draws the exact lines of the plate boundaries.

reason: Expansion changes volume, not mass.
en: Keep the room temperature steady while weighing liquids, because warm liquids expand and change their volume.

reason: Times vary by debate format; not a universal rule.
en: In a structured debate, a moderator gives each team three minutes to speak and one minute for rebuttals.

reason: Not all debates require stating an ethical principle.
en: In a debate, each side must state the ethical principle they use, such as doing no harm or maximizing benefit.

reason: Plate speed depends on slab pull, not just oceanic area.
en: Plates carrying large areas of heavy oceanic crust move faster, because the dense sinking edge pulls the rest of the plate along behind it.

reason: Inactive volcanoes can have recorded eruptions; this sounds extinct.
en: An inactive volcano is one that has no recorded eruption and shows no signs of waking up, but it is still a volcano.

reason: Lava flows aren't always flat; towns often build for fertile soil.
en: Many Philippine towns are built on the old lava flows of inactive volcanoes, because the land is flat and easy to build on.

reason: 29.5 days is phase cycle; orbital period is 27.3 days.
en: Earth spins once every 24 hours, while the Moon circles Earth once every 29.5 days, so we see the Sun rise daily but moon phases slowly.

reason: Rainforest soils are nutrient-poor but often deep, not thin.
en: Tropical rainforest soil is thin and poor because most nutrients are stored in the plants themselves, not in the ground.

reason: Streak test is for minerals, not whole rocks.
en: The streak test rubs a rock on a white porcelain tile to see the color of its powder, which is more reliable than surface color.

reason: Fizz indicates carbonate, not specifically calcite.
en: To test for calcite, a teacher places a drop of dilute acid on the rock; if it fizzes, the rock contains calcite.

reason: Metamorphic rocks can also show layers/foliation.
en: Many rock keys first ask if the rock has visible layers; this separates sedimentary rocks from igneous and metamorphic ones.

reason: Hardness compares tools scratching rocks, not rocks scratching each other.
en: A fair hardness test uses the same set of scratch tools on every rock, so you can compare which rocks scratch each other.

reason: Pin moves faster than ball; ball barely slows.
en: A bowling ball hitting a pin is nearly elastic: the pin flies off with most of the ball's speed while the heavy ball keeps rolling slowly.

reason: Zambales formed mainly by subduction, not Palawan collision.
en: The collision of the Palawan microcontinent with the western Philippines formed the Zambales and Mindoro mountains, adding land to the archipelago.

reason: Falling drops are precipitation, not condensation.
en: To measure condensation, count the drops that fall from the plastic wrap in one minute and record the number in a table.

reason: Precipitation may not occur within one hour; timing varies.
en: Observing the model every 10 minutes for an hour shows the sequence of evaporation, condensation, and precipitation in order.

reason: Collisions require touching; magnets repel without contact, not a collision.
en: A collision in physics does not need objects to touch; two magnets repelling each other without contact still exchange momentum and change each other's motion.

reason: Risk combines hazard and exposure; distance matters, so statement misleads.
en: A volcano's risk to a town depends on how many people and buildings are in the danger zone, so a crowded city far away can be riskier than a small village near the volcano.

reason: Classroom microscopes usually can't resolve mitochondria shapes clearly.
en: Mitochondria are very small, so you need a high power lens to see their shapes.

reason: Movement shows cytoplasmic streaming, not that fluid is alive.
en: In the cytoplasm, you might see tiny moving particles, which shows the fluid is alive and active.

reason: Periodic table gives symbols, not subscripts; subscripts come from bonding.
en: Scientists use a periodic table to find the correct symbols and subscripts for each element before writing any formula equation.

reason: Mitochondria usually not visible with classroom microscopes.
en: Start with the lowest power objective to find your specimen, then switch to higher power to see details like mitochondria.

reason: Need special staining, not just high power/lighting.
en: Mitochondria are tiny and almost colorless, so you need high power and good lighting to see their rod-like shapes.

reason: Heft suggests high density, not specifically iron; iron isn't a mineral.
en: Lifting a rock to feel if it is heavy for its size hints that it contains dense minerals like iron.

reason: Largest grain can misrepresent overall grain size; use typical grains.
en: Measuring the largest grain with a ruler helps you decide if the rock is coarse grained or fine grained.

reason: A key only works for rocks it includes; not universal.
en: The same dichotomous key works on rocks from any place, including volcanic rocks found near Taal and Mayon.

reason: Water vapor is invisible; clear container shows condensation, not vapor.
en: A water cycle model works best in a clear plastic container, because you can see the vapor, drops, and water level without opening it.

reason: Level surface spreads water evenly; drops won't gather in corner.
en: Set the model on a flat, level surface so the water spreads evenly and the collected drops gather in one predictable corner.

reason: Stages are continuous, not fixed morning-to-afternoon order.
en: Leave the model in a sunny spot for a whole day, so you can observe all four stages happen in order from morning to afternoon.

reason: Dye doesn't evaporate; condensed water stays clear.
en: Add a drop of food coloring to the water in the model, so you can trace the path of the liquid as it moves through the cycle.

reason: Gas particles collide often; 'barely' is misleading.
en: Most of a gas is empty space, because its particles are spread so far apart that they barely bump into each other.

reason: Not all solids; amorphous solids lack regular pattern.
en: In a solid, particles are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern, while in liquids and gases the arrangement is random.

reason: Water vapor is invisible; visible vapor is already condensation.
en: To predict the next stage, watch the water level drop and the vapor appear, then say 'condensation will happen next'.

reason: Lower epidermis peel mostly lacks chloroplasts; use mesophyll/Elodea.
en: To see chloroplasts, a thin layer from the underside of a leaf is peeled and mounted in a drop of water on a slide.

reason: Kidneys are organs, not tubes; urinary tract excludes kidneys.
en: The urinary tract is a tube system—kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra—that works together to store and remove urine.

reason: Deep quakes occur along subducting slab, not just near trench.
en: In the Philippines, shallow earthquakes happen along the fault zones, while deep earthquakes happen near the trenches, showing two different boundary types.

reason: Himalayas are young, still rising from ongoing collision.
en: Major mountain belts like the Himalayas mark old continental collisions, while active volcanoes and earthquakes show where plates are moving today.

reason: Three seeds per pot is replication, not full experiment repeat.
en: Repeat the experiment with three seeds per pot and take the average to make results more reliable.

reason: Not all reptiles lay eggs; some give live birth.
en: Reptiles have dry, scaly skin and lay eggs with leathery shells, like snakes and turtles, and they are cold-blooded.

reason: Toads have dry, bumpy skin, not smooth/moist.
en: Amphibians have moist, smooth skin that helps them breathe, and they usually stay near water, like frogs and toads.

reason: Non-flowering conifers produce seeds; flowers are the key trait.
en: Plants are classified as flowering or non-flowering by whether they produce flowers and seeds, like mango versus moss.

reason: Only works for opposite forces; angled forces need vector sum.
en: To check if forces are balanced, compare arrows pointing in opposite directions and see if their lengths match.

reason: Net force is vector sum, not just longer arrows' direction.
en: After comparing, draw one separate arrow to show the net force, pointing where the longer arrows point.

reason: Balanced forces can also mean constant motion, not just still.
en: Check your finished diagram by asking whether the object would stay still, speed up, or slow down from those arrows.

reason: Same packet gives same variety, not identical genetics.
en: Use seeds from the same packet to ensure all plants have the same genetic background.

reason: Not every molecule; some water is chemically split.
en: The water molecules on Earth have been cycling for billions of years, so the water you drink is the same water dinosaurs drank.

reason: Clouds are liquid droplets, not water vapor.
en: Wind carries clouds across the sky, so water vapor from one place can fall as rain somewhere else.

reason: Omits solid ice/snow phase.
en: The water cycle is a closed loop: water never leaves Earth, it just changes from liquid to gas and back.

reason: Potential energy depends on reference; at lowest point often zero.
en: At the middle of its swing, a pendulum has both kinetic and potential energy, because it is moving and still has some height.

reason: Crust isn't thousands of km thick; only deeper layers are.
en: Earth's layers are thousands of kilometers thick, so drawing them at true size would need a page as wide as the planet, which is why we use a scale.

reason: Max continental crust is ~1.1% of radius, slightly over 1%.
en: The crust is less than 1% of Earth's radius, so on a scale drawing it is usually just a thin line or even invisible.

reason: Mantle/crust shell is ~45% of radius, not thin.
en: In a scale drawing, the core takes up about half of the circle's diameter, leaving the mantle and crust as a thin shell around it.

reason: 35 km is continental average, not global average.
en: Because the crust varies from 5 to 70 km thick, a scale drawing might use an average value like 35 km for simplicity.

reason: Cracks can initially let water in; runoff claim oversimplified.
en: When clay soil dries, it becomes hard and cracked, so water runs off instead of soaking in.

reason: Slightly off: ~13°/day relative to stars, ~12°/day relative to Sun.
en: The Moon moves about 13 degrees eastward each day relative to the Sun, which is why it rises later each night.

reason: Moon's heliocentric path is a slightly wavy orbit, not a line/loops.
en: The Moon's path through space is a wavy line because it circles Earth while Earth circles the Sun.

reason: Conflates digestive waste with metabolic waste; feces don't go to kidneys/lungs.
en: A flow chart of digestion and excretion shows food becoming nutrients in the small intestine, then wastes traveling through the blood to the kidneys and lungs.

reason: Oversimplified; liver and kidneys handle different substances, not just catch twice.
en: The liver checks the blood right after it leaves the intestines, and the kidneys check it again later, so wastes and toxins are caught twice.

reason: Thinking is an organ/system function, not a tissue-level job.
en: When cells are grouped into tissues, they can do jobs that a single cell cannot, like pumping blood or thinking.

reason: Lithosphere includes crust and uppermost mantle, not just upper mantle.
en: The lithosphere and asthenosphere are not extra layers but zones within the upper mantle, so a scale drawing shows them as parts of the mantle's thickness.

reason: Net force zero doesn't mean each arrow has an opposite twin.
en: For an object that is not moving, every force arrow in the diagram must have a matching arrow of equal length pointing the opposite way.

reason: A slowing ball isn't pushed forward; friction acts backward.
en: A free-body diagram for a ball rolling across the floor and slowing down shows a longer friction arrow pointing backward and a shorter push arrow pointing forward.

reason: Unexpected results are useful, but not automatically the true answer.
en: Even if the results do not match what you expected, the investigation is a success because you learned the true answer.

reason: CO2 has polar bonds; both oxygens are slightly negative, dipoles cancel.
en: In carbon dioxide, the two oxygen atoms pull electrons equally from both sides, so the molecule has no slightly positive or negative ends.

reason: Ambiguous; covalent bonds are within water, not between molecules.
en: Every living thing on Earth, including plants and people in the Philippines, is mostly made of water molecules held together by covalent bonds.

reason: Liquid water lacks lattice, but ice forms one.
en: Water is a covalent compound: each H2O molecule is a separate unit, and many molecules stay near each other but do not form a lattice.

reason: Not all covalent compounds; network solids like diamond are continuous.
en: In a ball-and-stick model, an ionic compound looks like a 3D grid of alternating balls, while a covalent compound looks like separate small clusters.

reason: Oxygen gas is an element, not a compound.
en: Oxygen gas is a covalent compound made of separate O2 molecules that move freely, not a repeating lattice like salt.

reason: Biosphere and ecosystem include nonliving parts, not just cells.
en: Every level from a cell to the biosphere is made of cells, because all living things are made of cells and the biosphere contains all living things.

reason: Most body cells have two sets, so ~6 billion base pairs.
en: A human cell's DNA contains about 3 billion base pairs, enough to fill about 3,000 books with 1,000 pages each.

reason: DNA is tightly packed, not spread out; charge aids solubility.
en: The phosphate groups in DNA's backbone carry a negative charge, which helps DNA dissolve and stay spread out in the watery cell.

reason: Side also depends on waxing/waning phase, not just hemisphere.
en: The crescent moon's lit side points toward the Sun, but which side is lit (right or left) depends on whether you are in the Northern or Southern Hemisphere.

reason: Phrase 'fair weather observation' ambiguous; means fair-test observation, not clear weather.
en: A fair weather observation keeps the same place and the same time every day, changing only what the weather does.

reason: Species don't live hundreds of millions of years; body forms do.
en: The time scale reveals that some species, like certain shellfish, stayed almost the same for hundreds of millions of years, while others changed quickly.

reason: Only true with one known force; otherwise balance net force.
en: For an object at rest, draw any unknown force (like friction) with the same length as the known applied force but pointing the opposite way.

reason: Not every step needs a specific amount or time.
en: Write each step in the method with a specific amount and time, like 'add 10 drops' or 'wait 2 minutes'.

reason: Accurate but too advanced for grade 5.
en: Hydrogen is an exception to the octet rule: it needs only two electrons to be stable, so in water each hydrogen shares one pair with oxygen.

reason: Accurate but too advanced for grade 5.
en: In a covalent bond, the shared pair of electrons is attracted to both nuclei at once, and that pull is what holds the atoms together in water and carbon dioxide.

reason: Hemisphere-dependent; wording oversimplifies seasonal sunrise position shifts.
en: The Sun rises and sets at different points on the horizon each day, moving north in summer and south in winter.

reason: Longest day true, but earliest sunrise/latest sunset often not on solstice.
en: On the summer solstice, the Sun rises earliest and sets latest, giving the maximum daylight hours for that latitude.

reason: Striker should be held above barrel, not side.
en: To light a Bunsen burner, close the air hole first, hold the striker to the side of the barrel, and open the gas valve slowly.

reason: FaultFinder mainly shows faults; landslide layers may be separate.
en: Steep mountain slopes near a fault can slide during an earthquake, so the FaultFinder map also shows landslide-prone areas.

reason: Gaps are in rock layers, not the time scale itself.
en: The geologic time scale shows gaps where rock layers are missing, so scientists know that some parts of Earth's history are not recorded.

reason: Liquid water molecules are close, not separate clusters; wording misleads.
en: A space-filling model of salt shows spheres packed tightly in a grid, while a model of water shows separate clusters with empty space around them.

reason: Ion sizes predict structure, not always macroscopic crystal shape.
en: The pattern of ions in an ionic crystal is so orderly that scientists can predict its shape from the sizes of the ions.

reason: Dog ear shape is polygenic, not a simple recessive trait.
en: In dogs, the allele for floppy ears is recessive to pointy ears, so a floppy-eared dog must have two floppy alleles.

reason: Hammer and nail don't stick; collision is inelastic, not perfectly.
en: A hammer hitting a nail is inelastic because the hammer keeps moving with the nail and much of the energy goes into pushing the wood apart.

reason: Faults are zones; verification uses more than walking GPS.
en: Scientists verify the FaultFinder map by walking the fault trace on the ground with a GPS device and marking the exact line.

reason: Shows age/recency, not always an exact date.
en: The FaultFinder map lets you click on a fault line to see its name and the date of its last known movement.

reason: Mountains are landforms made of many rocks, not single rocks.
en: Rocks are hard, solid pieces of the Earth made of minerals, and they come in many sizes from tiny pebbles to huge mountains.

reason: Diamond is a mineral, not a rock.
en: Some rocks are soft and crumble easily, like chalk, while others are very hard, like diamond.

reason: Rust is iron oxide; other metals corrode differently.
en: Metals can rust when they stay wet, like the brown rust on an old iron nail.

reason: Too advanced for grade 5; transition metals break pattern.
en: Moving from left to right across a period, each element adds one more outer electron, which is why properties change gradually across the row.

reason: Helium exception: group 18 has two outer electrons, not eight.
en: Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, so they react in similar ways, like lithium and sodium both being soft metals.

reason: Not true for helium or transition metal groups.
en: Elements in the same period have the same number of shells but different outer electron counts, while elements in the same group share the same outer count.

reason: Not true for transition metals; inner d electrons matter.
en: An element's group is decided by its outer electrons only, not by the total number of electrons in the atom.

reason: Not always; 4s fills before 3d in transition metals.
en: Electrons fill the innermost shell first, then the next, and this filling order is what gives each element its row and column.

reason: Not all living things breathe air; fish use water's oxygen.
en: Living things need the oxygen in air to breathe, and fire also needs oxygen to keep burning.

reason: Scale should attach at effort point, not load.
en: To measure how a lever changes force, attach a spring scale to the load and read the number of newtons it takes to lift it.

reason: Same people's weights stay constant; force isn't actually measured.
en: A class can use a seesaw as a lever, keeping the same two people on it while moving the fulcrum to test how force changes.

reason: Keeping effort distance same while changing lever length may not affect force.
en: To compare two different levers fairly, use the same load and the same effort distance, and only change the length of the lever itself.

reason: Widow's peak isn't simple single-gene; oversimplified.
en: In humans, a widow's peak hairline is dominant over a straight hairline, so a child with two straight-hairline parents will have a straight hairline.

reason: Tongue rolling isn't simple Mendelian; non-rollers can have roller children.
en: The ability to roll the tongue is dominant over not rolling it, so two non-rollers cannot have a roller child.

reason: Lifted warning means threat passed; stay away until official all-clear.
en: After a tsunami warning is lifted, people must still stay away from the coast because the danger can last for many hours.

reason: Protists aren't all single-celled; classification uses more than microscope.
en: The six-kingdom system gives single-celled life its own kingdoms, because a microscope shows protists are very different from plants and animals.

reason: Opening windows risks broken glass; only doors are standard.
en: After the shaking stops, the plan says to open doors and windows because the quake may have jammed them shut.

reason: Largest grain isn't representative; measure typical or average grain size.
en: To measure grain crystal size, place a ruler against the rock and record the width of the largest visible grain in millimeters.

reason: Scientists classify rocks by origin and composition, not this fixed order.
en: Scientists sort rocks into groups by first separating them by grain size, then by color, and finally by texture.

reason: Packing/gaps describes texture, not crystal pattern.
en: To see if crystals have a pattern, look at the rock under a hand lens and note if the grains are packed tightly or have gaps.

reason: Dim bulb means partial resistance, not complete blocking.
en: A brighter bulb means the material conducts electricity well, while a dim bulb or no light means the material blocks the current.

reason: Below one reduces force, not just changes direction.
en: Compare the mechanical advantage to one: a number above one means the lever multiplied your force, and below one means it only changed direction.

reason: Should be vector sum of velocities; speeds add only when aligned.
en: An airplane flying with a tailwind has a faster ground speed, but its velocity is the sum of its own speed and the wind's speed.

reason: Water drop tests absorption, not porosity.
en: To test porosity, scientists drop water on a fresh surface and watch whether it soaks in quickly, slowly, or beads up on top.

reason: Cooling rate only applies to igneous rocks.
en: Scientists record whether a rock looks like a solid mass or is made of visible grains, because that tells if it cooled fast or slow.

reason: Not every projectile rises then falls; horizontal/downward launches don't.
en: The path of every projectile is a parabola, a symmetric curved shape that rises to one peak and then falls back down.

reason: Speed also matters, not just release angle.
en: When a player shoots a basketball, the ball's arc from hands to hoop is a projectile path, and the release angle decides whether the shot reaches the rim.

reason: Only past 45°; below that, steeper can land farther.
en: Water sprayed from a garden hose follows a projectile arc, so tilting the hose steeper makes the water rise higher but land closer.

reason: Angle correct; steeper isn't always wasteful—45° maximizes range at same speed.
en: Long jumpers take off at about 20 degrees above the ground, because a steeper angle would waste energy going upward instead of forward.

reason: Charcoal conducts poorly; may not light a typical bulb.
en: Charcoal, like the kind used for cooking, is a form of carbon that can conduct electricity and light a bulb in a circuit tester.

reason: Wet string conducts little; usually too weak to light bulb.
en: A dry string is an insulator, but a wet string can conduct a little electricity, so it can light the bulb dimly.

reason: His list included some compounds like lime and silica.
en: Antoine Lavoisier made one of the first lists of pure elements, separating true elements from mixtures and compounds.

reason: Earlier charts existed but were incomplete or not widely accepted.
en: Before the periodic table, scientists had no single chart to compare all known elements at a glance, so discoveries were hard to link.

reason: Rows show periods/shell number, not a repeating pattern.
en: In the periodic table, columns group elements with similar properties, while rows show a repeating pattern of electron shells.

reason: Three-domain system is based on rRNA, not DNA.
en: The six-kingdom system groups organisms by their cell type and how they get food, making it simpler for students than the DNA-based three-domain system.

reason: Understates: bacteria/archaea are separate domains, plants/animals same domain.
en: The three-domain system shows that bacteria and archaea are as different from each other as animals are from plants.

reason: Antibiotics also affect helpful bacteria, not only harmful ones.
en: Knowing that archaebacteria and eubacteria have different cell walls helps scientists develop antibiotics that target only harmful bacteria.

reason: Two divisions alone don't halve chromosomes; first division separates pairs.
en: The reason meiosis produces four cells instead of two is that it divides twice, which is why each sex cell ends up with half the original chromosomes.

reason: Speed can be zero, so not always positive.
en: Speed is always a positive number, but velocity can be negative when an object moves backward or opposite a chosen direction.

reason: Resultant is 1 m/s west, not east.
en: When two velocities combine, you add them like arrows, so 3 m/s east plus 4 m/s east is 7 m/s east, but 3 m/s east plus 4 m/s west is 1 m/s east.

reason: For same speed, 70° and 20° have equal range.
en: A projectile launched at a steep angle, like 70 degrees, follows a tall narrow arc, while a flat 20-degree launch makes a low, wide arc.

reason: At 60°, upward component is about 87%, not half.
en: At a 30-degree launch, about 87% of the launch speed goes forward, but at a 60-degree launch, only half goes forward and the rest goes upward.

reason: Overstates: not all animals are trapped or unable to survive.
en: When roads and farms split a forest into small patches, animals are trapped in tiny areas with too little food, space, and mates to survive.

reason: Full perimeter walk returns to start; displacement is zero.
en: A farmer walking along the edges of a square rice field travels a distance equal to the perimeter, but his displacement is the diagonal across the field.

reason: Displacement is straight-line start-to-finish, not just height gained.
en: A car climbing a long winding mountain road to Baguio covers many kilometers of distance, but its displacement is just the straight height gained.

reason: Stability is maintaining ecosystem structure/function, not just providing services.
en: Ecosystem stability means the place keeps providing food, clean water, and shelter even when conditions like drought or flood change.

reason: Drought may kill other crops too; 'do not starve' too absolute.
en: When a drought kills the main food crop, a farm with many crops still has other plants to eat, so people and animals do not starve.

reason: Other species may also get sick; animals can lose food.
en: If a disease wipes out one species in a diverse forest, the other species stay healthy, so the forest keeps standing and feeding its animals.

reason: Storms can destroy all forest layers; diversity doesn't guarantee shelter.
en: When many species share a forest, they use different parts of it, so a storm does not destroy all the shelter at once.

reason: Pest could attack all varieties; 'only a part' too absolute.
en: A rice field with only one variety can lose everything to a single pest, while a field with many varieties loses only a part.

reason: Zambales are mainly ophiolite/obducted oceanic crust, not just volcanic rocks.
en: The Zambales Mountains in western Luzon are made of volcanic rocks that came from an older subduction zone, showing how plate motion builds mountains.

reason: Distemper spreads from domestic dogs, not farm animals.
en: Diseases from farm animals, like distemper, can jump to wild lions and dogs, killing many in a short time and pushing them toward extinction.

reason: Dry ice forms a molecular crystal lattice.
en: Dry ice is a covalent solid made of separate CO2 molecules, so it has no crystal lattice, unlike ionic salt.

reason: Same material assumed; otherwise specific heat matters.
en: The same amount of heat raises a small object's temperature more than a large one, because temperature change depends on mass.

reason: Heat isn't stored; pot has more thermal energy.
en: A drop of boiling water and a full pot of boiling water have the same temperature, but the pot holds much more heat because it has more particles.

reason: Not all predators can switch prey; some are specialized.
en: In a diverse ecosystem, a predator that loses its usual prey can switch to another available species, so it survives food shortages without starving.

reason: Not all animals can eat insects or alternative foods.
en: When a favorite fruit is scarce in a diverse forest, animals can eat seeds, leaves, or insects instead, so they do not starve.

reason: Group 13–18 need last digit, not full number.
en: To know an element's valence electrons, just look at its group number in the main part of the periodic table.

reason: Only true for main-group periods; transition metals differ.
en: Across a period, the number of valence electrons increases from one to eight, which is why properties change gradually.

reason: Chlorine disinfects; fluoride prevents tooth decay, not safety.
en: Fluorine and chlorine are both group 17 elements, and compounds of them are used to keep drinking water safe.

reason: Reactivity trend varies; halogens decrease down group.
en: Elements in the same group have the same valence electrons, but those lower down have more shells, so they react faster even though they react in the same way.

reason: Group number doesn't always equal valence electrons; e.g., group 13 has 3.
en: The periodic table is deliberately arranged so that elements with the same valence electron count stack in the same column, which is why the group number matches that count.

reason: Modern 18 columns also include transition metals, not just noble gases.
en: Mendeleev's original table had 8 columns, while the modern one has 18 because noble gases were added later.

reason: Rising air cools adiabatically; condensation releases heat, not drains it.
en: When typhoon winds push against a mountain, the air rises and cools, which drains some of the storm's heat energy and weakens it.

reason: Misleading; table maps elements, not full atom electron arrangement.
en: The electron structure explains why the periodic table is a map of the atom, showing how electrons are arranged in shells and blocks.

reason: Seismic speeds alone don't reveal composition; other evidence needed.
en: The core is about twice as dense as the mantle, so seismic wave speeds tell scientists it is made of heavy metals like iron and nickel.

reason: Many, not all, stratovolcanoes are andesitic.
en: Stratovolcanoes are made of andesite, a rock with medium silica, which makes their lava sticky enough to build tall, steep layers.

reason: Slope alone is not definitive; other factors matter.
en: The steepness of a volcano's cone is a clue to its magma's stickiness, so scientists can guess the rock type just by looking at the slope.

reason: Burning wood is combustion, not a simple combination reaction.
en: Combination reactions often release energy as heat and light, which is why burning wood in a campfire is a combination reaction between wood and oxygen.

reason: Mentions four types but only describes three; omits single vs double.
en: The four reaction types differ by what happens to the reactants: combination joins them, decomposition splits one, and replacement swaps atoms or ions.

reason: Omits ice, temperature changes, plant roots as breaking forces.
en: A rock breaks into smaller pieces only when wind, water, or people act on it, not by itself.

reason: Assumes stationary car also 1,000 kg; otherwise final speed differs.
en: A 1,000-kilogram car moving at 10 meters per second has 10,000 units of momentum, and if it sticks to a stationary car, both move at 5 meters per second together.

reason: Earth moves downward, not upward; momentum change is opposite ball's.
en: When a basketball bounces off the floor, the Earth itself moves upward a tiny bit, so the total momentum of ball and Earth stays conserved.

reason: Fossils mostly in sedimentary rocks; rare exceptions exist.
en: Fossils are found only in sedimentary rocks, so scientists use them to date those layers, not rocks that melted or were squeezed.

reason: Younger rocks can also contain only simple fossils.
en: Simple single-celled fossils are the oldest known, so a rock layer with only simple fossils is likely from early Earth.

reason: Pebbles can change shape by weathering and erosion.
en: A tadpole grows into a frog, changing its body shape, but a pebble stays the same shape forever because it is not alive.

reason: True but too advanced for grade 5.
en: When two objects collide at an angle and then move off in different directions, the total momentum is still conserved, but you must add their momenta as vectors.

reason: Respiration breaks down glucose using oxygen; oxygen isn't broken down.
en: Photosynthesis makes glucose and oxygen in chloroplasts, while respiration breaks them down in mitochondria to release energy.

reason: Units depend on axes; m/s only for meter-second axes.
en: The speed from a distance-time graph is in meters per second, so a uniform velocity line rising 10 meters in 2 seconds has a speed of 5 meters per second.

reason: Steady speed alone doesn't ensure constant direction.
en: A boat moving at a steady speed on a calm river shows uniform velocity, and its distance-time graph is a straight line.

reason: Neutrality also requires equal protons, not electrons alone.
en: Electrons, which have a negative charge, zoom around the nucleus in a cloud, making the atom electrically neutral overall.

reason: Models aren't only pictures; can be physical, mathematical, or computer.
en: A scientific model is a simplified picture that helps explain something too big, too small, or too slow to see directly.

reason: Valves don't pump blood; chambers do.
en: A model of the human heart shows the chambers and valves that pump blood, even though the real heart is inside the body.

reason: Gamma wavelengths are smaller than atoms, not atomic nuclei.
en: Radio waves can be as long as a building, while gamma rays are smaller than an atom's nucleus.

reason: Monotremes like platypus lay eggs, not live birth.
en: Mammals are born alive from their mother's body and drink her milk, which gives them food and strength to grow.

reason: Monotremes lay eggs; conifers produce seeds in cones, not fruits.
en: Mammals give birth to live young, birds lay eggs outside their bodies, and plants produce seeds inside fruits.

reason: Omits carbon dioxide; not all mature plants flower.
en: A mature plant has roots, a stem, leaves, and flowers, and it can make its own food using sunlight and water.

reason: Top point isn't necessarily tracing a circle; it's rotational motion.
en: A spinning top on the floor shows uniform circular motion because its top point traces a circle at a steady rate.

reason: Acceleration is change in velocity, not direction alone, divided by time.
en: To find acceleration, you divide the change in speed or direction by the time it took for that change to happen.

reason: Basketball spins in place; that's rotational motion, not uniform circular motion.
en: A basketball spinning on a finger is in uniform circular motion because its surface moves in a circle.

reason: Shells are energy levels/regions, not actual circular paths.
en: Electron shells are the circular paths drawn around the nucleus, showing where electrons are found.

reason: Egg white isn't layered; shells are discrete energy levels.
en: The nucleus is like the yolk of an egg, while the electron shells are like the layers of white around it.

reason: Not all boundaries are fossil-based; some are rock/climate changes.
en: The geologic time scale is divided into eons, eras, periods, and epochs, and each boundary marks a major change seen in the fossil record.

reason: Only if initially at rest; otherwise it keeps moving.
en: If two people push a box from opposite sides with equal force, the forces cancel, giving zero net force and zero acceleration, so the box stays still.

reason: Gravity's tangential pull, not string tension, accelerates it at end.
en: A pendulum at the end of its swing has zero speed for an instant, but it still accelerates because the string's pull changes its direction.

reason: Antacid use isn't due to heat resistance; it neutralizes acid.
en: Magnesium oxide is a white powder used in antacids and fireproof materials because it resists high heat.

reason: Most meteorites come from asteroids; comets rarely produce meteorites.
en: Meteorites that fall to Earth are direct samples of asteroids or comets, letting scientists study the solar system's earliest materials in a lab.

reason: Factually correct but too advanced for grade 5.
en: A force makes an object accelerate, and that acceleration must last for some time to change the object's speed and therefore its momentum.

reason: Factually correct but too advanced for grade 5.
en: A rocket engine pushes with a steady force for minutes, so the rocket's momentum builds up gradually until it reaches a very high speed.

reason: Factually correct but too advanced for grade 5.
en: Gravity pulls a falling mango for every second it drops, so its momentum increases steadily until it reaches the ground.

reason: Brief sideways push adds perpendicular velocity, increasing speed.
en: A sideways force on a moving ball acts for a short time, changing the ball's direction of momentum without changing its speed.

reason: Deep-sea vent food webs use chemosynthesis, not sunlight.
en: The sun is the original energy source for every food pyramid, because green plants capture its light to make their own food.

reason: Compass shows seasonal north/south shift, not fixed east/west.
en: Using a compass to record where the Sun rises and sets shows that it always rises in the east and sets in the west.

reason: Only true for groups 1–2; groups 13–18 need subtract 10.
en: For main-group elements, the group number equals the number of outer electrons, so group 2 elements have two outer electrons.

reason: Period 4 length due to filling 3d, not just shell capacity.
en: Periods have different lengths because each new electron shell can hold more electrons, so period 2 has 8 elements and period 4 has 18.

reason: Wood shows magnetic core needed, not specifically iron.
en: Replace the iron nail with a wooden pencil and the coil picks up almost no paper clips, proving iron is needed.

reason: Identity comes from protons, not unchanged inner electrons.
en: Only the outer-shell electrons take part in ion formation; the inner electrons stay unchanged, so the ion keeps its identity as the same element.

reason: Boundary is a circle, not straight; tilt changes orientation.
en: A model with a tilted globe and a lamp shows that the circle of illumination is tilted, so the day-night boundary is not a straight line.

reason: Before winter solstice day length decreases, not increases.
en: The length of daytime increases at the same rate before and after the winter solstice, and decreases at the same rate before and after the summer solstice.

reason: Lit half is the half facing the Sun; tilt doesn't change that.
en: A model with a tilted globe and a flashlight shows that the lit half is not the same as the half facing the Sun because of the tilt.

reason: Not always; near June noon shadow points south, moving counterclockwise.
en: In the Philippines, a shadow stick's shadow turns clockwise from west to north to east as the Sun moves across the sky.
